title: A " Study " Has Begun On the Affects of the Lambeth Experiment On Children: The Answers Are Obvious, And Reassuring, But the Questions Are Really Frightening.

content_html_sanitized:
Posted June 28, 2002
(MarijuanaNews note: Although it might not make a popular song, I think that what the world needs now must surely be " critical thinking skills. "

I spend so much time reading prohibitionist propaganda that I should be inured to irrationality. And generally, when the nonsense comes from the usual suspects, it sometimes even amuses me. In fact, when they make complete fools of themselves, as they so often do, I am delighted to help them get their message out.

However, when people who do not work directly for the prohibitionist propaganda agencies write something like this example from the BBC, I am terribly concerned about the ability of a democratic society to govern itself.

What follows is largely just a series of variations on the prohibitionist cliché about " sending the wrong message to children " that is used to oppose any lessening of the war on cannabis users -- in whatever circumstances.

But it goes far beyond that in displaying a lack of critical thinking skills, not only in the media, and the police force, but in broad segments of society.

The fact that any sincere concerns about the consequences liberalizing cannabis policies in the UK could be addressed empirically by just looking at the Dutch experience, makes this more absurd. And unlike people in DEAland, the Brits actually know where Holland is!
See

However, while the results of the Brixton/Lambeth experiment are very encouraging, it is the lack of simple common sense and elementary logic reflected in the questions that really frightens me.)

From BBC News
June 25, 2002

The cannabis scheme aimed to free up police time

A study has begun to find out the effects of a " softly, softly " cannabis police policy on children in south London. It comes after evidence pupils believe cannabis has been legalised since the policy was introduced and some as young as nine have smoked the drug.
(MarijuanaNews note: I have no idea what the " evidence pupils believe cannabis has been legalized " might be. But let's assume that such misconceptions are widespread. Indeed, let's assume that all of the children in the area think that cannabis is legal, and that cannabis is about to become the national flower of the UK, and that Her Majesty is requesting that all of the bouquets that are presented to her should contain cannabis, just like the one given to her by Colin Davies.

Now, let's think about Scotch whiskey. It is completely " legal " in the UK. Its name rightly implies that the Scots are proud of this product identified with their ancient land and for which there is a global market. I am certain that it is served at The Palace, and is consumed by at least some members of the Royal Family. What does that tell us about children and Scotch?

Absolutely nothing!)

The policy pilot was introduced in Lambeth by Metropolitan police commander Brian Paddick in 2001, sees those in possession of the drug warned instead of arrested.

The area's new police chief Brian Moore said all schools in the borough were being surveyed about the effects on youngsters.

Mr Moore, who replaced Commander Paddick after he was moved to a desk job at Scotland Yard, said: " Some opinion formers have raised concerns more children of the nine and 10-year-old level are taking cannabis than before the pilot. "
(MarijuanaNews note: The phrase " some opinion formers " is very interesting. But, let's assume that " more children of the nine and 10-year-old level are taking cannabis than before the pilot. " Post pilot ergo propter pilot?

Implicit in the question is the fact that nine year-olds have been using cannabis before the pilot. What a triumph of prohibition! Even if the trend has accelerated that would prove nothing except that prohibition is a disastrous failure.)

Lambeth's 66 primary and 10 secondary schools are being asked whether they have excluded more children for cannabis since the scheme began.

They are also being asked whether more cannabis and drug paraphernalia has been found.

What would that prove? That the schools have increase surveillance and/or the use of exclusion? That students are being less careful in hiding their use? Or that they think that not arresting adults for doing something means that it is okay for kids to do it at school?

Of course, it is just exactly that idea that the prohibitionists are pushing. But if that is the case, does this imply a problem with cannabis policies or a problem with the educational system?)

Experts' assessment

Mr Moore said: " The feedback is very clear so far that there has been no escalation, which I think is a re-assuring response to some of the concerns. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Oh my, perhaps the children are not as lacking in critical thinking skills as the adults! If that is the case, at what age does the " education " disaster deprive them of their thinking skills?)

He has asked for 25 experts, including educationalists, teachers, youth workers and drugs workers to look at the scheme.

They will look into whether there is any evidence of the pilot affecting the health of children.
(MarijuanaNews note: How in less than a year -- would the health of children be affected by a policy of not arresting adults?)

There have also been claims of people being drawn into Lambeth to buy and sell cannabis as a result of the scheme.
(MarijuanaNews note: At last, a rational question. As it happens the answer again appears to be " no. " But if people had been " drawn into Lambeth to buy and sell cannabis as a result of the scheme, " what would that prove?

It would merely prove that limiting tolerance to a small area concentrates the problems of prohibition in that area. This is what I call the Needle Park syndrome.)

Hundreds warned

But Deputy Assistant Commissioner Mike Fuller said: " There is no discernible difference in terms of the number of people we are finding in possession of cannabis compared to before the pilot. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Fuller is a prohibitionist, who has been raising some of the absurd questions about the pilot.

There are two reason that this may not have happened.

First, cannabis appears to be readily available in all areas of London, and Brixton is a bit on the rough side, so people from other areas choose not to go there.

Second, despite all of the publicity and furor over the pilot, there were fewer people stopped for cannabis before the pilot than after. The police were only haphazardly enforcing the cannabis laws there before. All that the pilot has really done, is save the police a lot of time on the cannabis stops they make, and very importantly it has created a consistent policy, which is essential to any appearance of justice.)

A total of 1,190 people have been warned for possession since the scheme began last July.

Of those, 52.7% were from outside the borough, a similar proportion to those caught in possession before the pilot, suggesting people were not flooding into the area to buy drugs.
(MarijuanaNews note: It is important to remember that these warnings are accompanied by a confiscation of the person's cannabis, which is dumped on the spot. Does this sound like cannabis is " legal "?

A brief article in today's London Times reports that arrests for cocaine and heroin had risen, and 1,200 extra " stop and searches " for suspected drug offences were made.

Why doesn't anyone ask what message that sends to children?)
